newsitem.title: USA: Clinton support seems solid with nine days to go.
newsitem.headline: Clinton support seems solid with nine days to go.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
President Bill Clinton poached votes in Republican-leaning Virginia on Sunday as Republican Bob Dole extended his stay in California in a long-odds bid to avert defeat.
Clinton embarked on a seven-state trip, starting with a rally in Virginia, one of several normally solid Republican southern states he has a reasonable chance of winning in the Nov. 5 election.
"Most people in Virginia have been voting against members of my party for president for over three decades now and I know how hard it is to break a habit," Clinton said.
"One of the things we all teach our kids is that some habits have to be broken," he said to laughter from the crowd.

The Reuters daily tracking poll showed Clinton increasing his lead over Dole among likely voters to 13.4 percentage points. The CNN/USA Today Gallup poll showed Clinton leading by 20 points. ABC television had Clinton 15 points in front.
If that kind of lead held until Election Day Clinton would be in position to score a landslide of historical proportions.
Republican pollster Robert Teeter said there was little reason for Dole to hope for a last-minute reverse in the final days of a campaign where Clinton's lead has stayed remarkably stable for months.
"There's no evidence that there's anything going on or changing. There's no dynamic in this election," he said.
The focus was turning to the battle for control of Congress, where Democrats were pushing to regain majorities two years after Republicans took control of the Senate and the House of Representatives.

"Everything I see gives me optimism that we will win both houses back. The Republicans botched a wonderful opportunity they had two years ago. They were radical. They were extreme," said Rep. Richard Gephardt of Missouri, who would become House Speaker if the Democrats took over.
But Republicans maintained that polls showed them with a reasonable chance of keeping control of both the Senate and the House.

Dole decided to stay an extra day in California, hoping to revive his challenge for the state's 54 Electoral College votes -- one fifth of the 270 needed to win the presidency in the U.S. indirect election system.

At a rally of Vietnamese-Americans in San Jose, Dole criticized Clinton for not doing enough to police the nation's borders and reiterated his support for a controverisal ballot initiative to end affirmative action and preferences in government hiring, contracting and school admissions.
"Thousands of Californians have been victims of violent criminals who should have been stopped at the borders before they ever set foot in America," Dole said.
"That is a price that people pay for the federal government's failure to secure the border," he said.

In recent days Dole's speeches turned increasingly sour and abrasive. He not only attacked the media but even the public for failing to pay attention to what Dole believed were Clinton's serious ethical shortcomings.
White House adviser George Stephanopoulos, interviewed on NBC's "Meet the Press," said Clinton and first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton had done nothing wrong.
"Bob Dole ought to apologize" for some of the claims he has made in recent days, Stephanopoulos said.
Reform Party candidate Ross Perot, stuck in single digits in the polls, maintained his own assault on Clinton's ethics in an interview on the same program.
"You should never let anyone be president of the United States who does not have a strong moral and ethical base," Perot said.

Dole's campaign manager Scott Reed said Dole was within striking distance in Ohio, Michigan and Missouri. The base of the party in the South was coming back to Dole and he was optimistic about the Rocky Mountain states.
But a poll in Ohio showed Clinton leading by nine points in a state every successful Republican presidential candidate has succeeded in carrying.
